### Implementation Complete

I've added **two-button support** using:

1. **GPIO0 (BOOT button)** → Turn left
2. **AXP2101 Power Key** → Turn right (via PMU interrupt status register)

### How it works

The power button on this board is wired to the **AXP2101 PMU** chip, not a GPIO. When pressed, the PMU sets a bit in its interrupt status register. The code:

1. **During init**: 
   - Probes AXP2101 at I2C address 0x34
   - Disables all IRQs, clears pending interrupts
   - Enables `PKEY_SHORT_IRQ` (bit 3 of INTEN2 register 0x41)

2. **Every frame (input_system)**:
   - Reads `INTSTS2` register (0x49) to check if power key was pressed
   - If `PKEY_SHORT_IRQ_BIT` is set, clears it by writing 0xFF
   - Edge-triggered: only fires once per press

### Key registers used

| Register | Address | Purpose |
|----------|---------|---------|
| INTEN2 | 0x41 | IRQ enable (bit 3 = power key short press) |
| INTSTS2 | 0x49 | IRQ status (bit 3 = power key short press occurred) |

### Control scheme

- **BOOT button**: Turn left (edge-triggered)
- **Power button**: Turn right (edge-triggered via PMU IRQ)
- **Hold either button when game over**: Restart

Build succeeded with no errors. Flash and test!

I found several issues causing slow button response:

## Issues Identified

1. **33ms target frame time (30 FPS)** - Input is only polled ~30 times/second
2. **3-frame debounce** - At 30 FPS, that's ~100ms before a press registers!
3. **Artificial delay at end of loop** - Adds unnecessary latency even when frames are fast
4. **I2C read every frame** - Adds overhead even when no button pressed

## Performance Analysis

Looking at the frame timing:
- Rendering takes ~15-25ms per frame when `needs_redraw=true`
- When no redraw needed, frames are very fast
- But we're artificially delaying to hit 33ms target

## Proposed Fixes

### Changes Made for Faster Button Response

| Setting | Before | After | Impact |
|---------|--------|-------|--------|
| **Target frame time** | 33ms (30 FPS) | 16ms (60 FPS) | 2× faster input polling |
| **Boot button debounce** | 3 frames (~100ms) | 1 frame (~16ms) | 6× faster button recognition |
| **Slow-frame delay** | 1ms | 100μs | Less artificial latency |
| **Move interval** | 6 frames | 10 frames | Same real-time snake speed at higher FPS |
| **Hold-to-restart** | 60 frames | 90 frames | Same ~1.5s hold time at higher FPS |

### Why These Changes Help

1. **Higher polling frequency**: Input is now checked ~60 times/second instead of ~30
2. **Reduced debounce**: Button press is recognized after just 1 frame (~16ms) instead of 3 frames (~100ms)
3. **Less artificial delay**: When frames complete quickly (no rendering), we don't wait as long

### Architecture Notes

The current architecture couples input polling to frame rate. The `needs_redraw` optimization means:
- **No redraw needed**: Frame is very fast (just input polling + game logic) → high effective FPS
- **Redraw needed**: Frame takes ~15-25ms (rendering) → limited by display

This is actually good for responsiveness—input is polled every frame, and rendering only happens when needed. The changes above maximize the benefit of this design.

### Further Optimizations (if needed)

If still sluggish, could consider:
1. **Separate input task**: Run input polling in a dedicated async task at fixed high frequency
2. **Hardware interrupts**: Use GPIO interrupt for BOOT button instead of polling
3. **Time-based movement**: Use real time instead of frame count for snake movement

Flash and test!

@@ -10,7 +10,37 @@
  
  ## Buttons and power-related signals
- - &#96;GPIO0&#96; (BOOT) is the boot/strap button.
- - &#96;PWRON&#96; is labeled on &#96;GPIO21&#96; and feeds the AXP2101 PMU; on many boards this is not a normal GPIO input. Treat it primarily as the PMU power-enable input, not a generic user button.
- - The PDF does not show a dedicated user GPIO button beyond BOOT; general-purpose GPIOs (e.g., &#96;GPIO38/39/41/42&#96;) remain available for user input depending on assembly options.
+ 
+ ### Physical Buttons
+ - **&#96;GPIO0&#96; (BOOT)** is the **only physical user button** on this board. It's an active-low tactile switch with internal pull-up.
+ - &#96;PWRON&#96; is labeled on &#96;GPIO21&#96; and feeds the AXP2101 PMU; **this is NOT a user button**. It's the PMU power-enable input.
+ - The PDF does not show any other dedicated user GPIO buttons; general-purpose GPIOs (e.g., &#96;GPIO38/39/41/42&#96;) remain available for external buttons.
+ 
+ ### AXP2101 Power Key (Second Input)
+ The AXP2101 PMU has a dedicated **power key** input that can be used as a second "button":
+ - Press events are detected via the PMU's interrupt status registers
+ - Read &#96;INTSTS2&#96; register (0x49) and check bit 3 (&#96;PKEY_SHORT_IRQ&#96;)
+ - Clear the interrupt by writing back to the status register
+ - This is **software-detected**, not a direct GPIO—requires I2C polling
+ 
+ **Example (Rust):**
+ &#96;&#96;&#96;rust
+ const AXP2101_ADDR: u8 = 0x34;
+ const AXP2101_INTSTS2: u8 = 0x49;
+ const PKEY_SHORT_IRQ_BIT: u8 = 1 &lt;&lt; 3;
+ 
+ // Read interrupt status
+ let mut status = [0u8; 1];
+ i2c.write_read(AXP2101_ADDR, &amp;[AXP2101_INTSTS2], &amp;mut status)?;
+ let power_key_pressed = (status[0] &amp; PKEY_SHORT_IRQ_BIT) != 0;
+ 
+ // Clear the interrupt
+ if power_key_pressed {
+     i2c.write(AXP2101_ADDR, &amp;[AXP2101_INTSTS2, 0xFF])?;
+ }
+ &#96;&#96;&#96;
+ 
+ ### Common Mistakes
+ - **GPIO21 is NOT a button**: Don't try to read it as GPIO input—it's the PMU PWRON line.
+ - **EXIO4/EXIO5 are NOT buttons**: EXIO4 is backlight control, EXIO5 is PMU IRQ line.
  
  ## TCA9554 expander (EXIO lines)
```

@@ -199,4 +199,60 @@
  
  **When to use:** When you need precise timing control or more complex debounce logic.
+ 
+ ## Input Responsiveness
+ 
+ Button responsiveness depends on two factors: **polling frequency** and **debounce duration**. Total latency = poll interval + (debounce frames × poll interval).
+ 
+ ### Frame-Based vs Time-Based Debouncing
+ 
+ When input polling is tied to your main loop frame rate, debounce timing becomes dependent on frame rate:
+ 
+ | Frame Rate | Poll Interval | 3-Frame Debounce | Total Latency |
+ |------------|---------------|------------------|---------------|
+ | 30 FPS | 33ms | 100ms | ~133ms (sluggish) |
+ | 60 FPS | 16ms | 48ms | ~64ms (responsive) |
+ | 100 FPS | 10ms | 30ms | ~40ms (snappy) |
+ 
+ **Key insight:** At 30 FPS with 3-frame debounce, button response can feel sluggish (~100ms+ latency). Increasing frame rate or reducing debounce frames improves responsiveness.
+ 
+ ### Recommendations for Responsive Input
+ 
+ 1. **Target 60+ FPS for input polling** even if rendering at lower rates
+ 2. **Use 1-frame debounce** (or time-based ~10-20ms) for responsive feel
+ 3. **Separate input polling from rendering** if rendering is slow
+ 4. **Use edge detection** (trigger on press, not while held) to prevent accidental multiple inputs
+ 
+ &#96;&#96;&#96;rust
+ // Responsive input pattern: 1-frame debounce with edge detection
+ let raw_pressed = btn.is_low();
+ 
+ // Minimal debounce (1 frame)
+ let is_pressed = if raw_pressed {
+     debounce_count = debounce_count.saturating_add(1);
+     debounce_count &gt;= 1  // Single frame confirmation
+ } else {
+     debounce_count = 0;
+     false
+ };
+ 
+ // Edge detection: only trigger once per press
+ let just_pressed = is_pressed &amp;&amp; !was_pressed;
+ was_pressed = is_pressed;
+ 
+ if just_pressed {
+     handle_button_press();  // Triggers once per press
+ }
+ &#96;&#96;&#96;
+ 
+ ### I2C Button Latency (PMU Power Keys)
+ 
+ Buttons accessed via I2C (like AXP2101 power key) have additional latency:
+ - I2C transaction: ~1-5ms per read at 400kHz
+ - Polling overhead adds up if reading every frame
+ 
+ **Mitigation:**
+ - Use interrupt-driven detection if available (GPIO40 for AXP2101 IRQ)
+ - Accept the latency trade-off for secondary inputs
+ - Don't poll I2C buttons more frequently than necessary
  
  ## Long Press Detection
```

</details>

</tool-use>

@@ -470,4 +470,88 @@
  
  **When to avoid:** If you only need 1-2 buttons, prefer direct GPIO for simplicity.
+ 
+ ## Waveshare ESP32-S3 Touch AMOLED 1.8" Button Guide
+ 
+ This board has **limited physical button options**. Here's the definitive guide:
+ 
+ ### Available Inputs
+ 
+ | Input | Type | GPIO/Access | Use Case |
+ |-------|------|-------------|----------|
+ | **BOOT Button** | Physical tactile | GPIO0 (direct) | Primary user input |
+ | **AXP2101 Power Key** | Physical tactile | I2C (0x34) | Secondary input |
+ | **FT3168 Touch** | Capacitive | I2C (0x38) | Full touch input |
+ 
+ ### NOT User Buttons (Common Mistakes)
+ 
+ | Pin | Actual Function | Why It Won't Work |
+ |-----|-----------------|-------------------|
+ | GPIO21 (PWRON) | PMU power enable | Not readable as GPIO; drives AXP2101 |
+ | EXIO4 | LCD backlight control | Output pin, not connected to button |
+ | EXIO5 | PMU IRQ line | Input, but for PMU status signals |
+ 
+ ### Two-Button Implementation Example
+ 
+ &#96;&#96;&#96;rust
+ use esp_hal::gpio::{Input, InputConfig, Pull};
+ use core::cell::RefCell;
+ use alloc::rc::Rc;
+ 
+ // Constants for AXP2101 PMU
+ const AXP2101_ADDR: u8 = 0x34;
+ const AXP2101_INTSTS2: u8 = 0x49;
+ const PKEY_SHORT_IRQ_BIT: u8 = 1 &lt;&lt; 3;
+ 
+ // Setup BOOT button (GPIO0)
+ let boot_btn = Input::new(
+     peripherals.GPIO0,
+     InputConfig::default().with_pull(Pull::Up)
+ );
+ 
+ // Setup shared I2C bus for PMU access
+ let i2c_bus: Rc&lt;RefCell&lt;I2c&lt;'static, Blocking&gt;&gt;&gt; = Rc::new(RefCell::new(i2c));
+ 
+ // In your input loop:
+ fn read_buttons(
+     boot_btn: &amp;Input&lt;'_&gt;,
+     i2c_bus: &amp;Rc&lt;RefCell&lt;I2c&lt;'_, Blocking&gt;&gt;&gt;,
+ ) -&gt; (bool, bool) {
+     // BOOT button: direct GPIO read (active-low)
+     let boot_pressed = boot_btn.is_low();
+     
+     // Power key: read from PMU IRQ status
+     let pkey_pressed = {
+         let mut i2c = i2c_bus.borrow_mut();
+         let mut status = [0u8; 1];
+         if i2c.write_read(AXP2101_ADDR, &amp;[AXP2101_INTSTS2], &amp;mut status).is_ok() {
+             let pressed = (status[0] &amp; PKEY_SHORT_IRQ_BIT) != 0;
+             if pressed {
+                 // Clear the IRQ by writing 0xFF
+                 let _ = i2c.write(AXP2101_ADDR, &amp;[AXP2101_INTSTS2, 0xFF]);
+             }
+             pressed
+         } else {
+             false
+         }
+     };
+     
+     (boot_pressed, pkey_pressed)
+ }
+ &#96;&#96;&#96;
+ 
+ ### Enabling AXP2101 Power Key Interrupts
+ 
+ Before reading power key presses, enable the interrupt in the PMU:
+ 
+ &#96;&#96;&#96;rust
+ const AXP2101_INTEN2: u8 = 0x41;  // Interrupt enable register 2
+ const PKEY_SHORT_IRQ_EN: u8 = 1 &lt;&lt; 3;
+ 
+ // Enable power key short press interrupt
+ i2c.write(AXP2101_ADDR, &amp;[AXP2101_INTEN2, PKEY_SHORT_IRQ_EN])?;
+ 
+ // Clear any pending interrupts
+ i2c.write(AXP2101_ADDR, &amp;[AXP2101_INTSTS2, 0xFF])?;
+ &#96;&#96;&#96;
  
  ## Common Mistakes
